October 10, 2026

Trump calls for Zelensky's ouster after friendly Putin call and Russian oil deal

tags: politics, war
sources: @aaronparnas

The Kremlin said a 90-minute call between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin was so cordial that neither leader wanted to end it first, and the call concluded with the lifting of sanctions allowing U.S. purchases of Russian oil. Hours after the deal, Russia launched a large overnight attack on Ukraine that killed more than a dozen people, including several children. Asked about the deaths, Trump said Ukraine needs a new president and called for Volodymyr Zelensky's removal, remarks reported to have been welcomed in Moscow. Critics have described the arrangement as treasonous, while Trump has promoted it as a win for the United States.

Army officers and service members resist planned live-streamed firing squad execution

tags: legal, politics, defence
sources: @aaronparnas, @oafnation_actual

Army officers have objected to a plan to live-stream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who is partially paralyzed and uses a wheelchair, warning it would cause irreparable generational harm; CNN reported the Army was blindsided by the live-stream decision. Service members are preparing religious exemption filings to avoid participating, and it is unclear whether officers may opt out. Democrats have united behind a push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the plan, and Pope has restated that the death penalty is inadmissible as an attack on human dignity. Republican Joe Kent said Hasan deserves to die but that broadcasting the execution is beneath the nation's dignity and would hand terrorists propaganda; the UN has described the plan as torture.

Hegseth ends anonymous military complaints as general officer ranks are cut

tags: defence, politics
sources: @total.hypocrisy

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a policy under which anonymous complaints within the military will generally no longer be considered, except for allegations of fraud, waste and abuse or specific credible evidence of substantial wrongdoing or danger to public health or safety. Commanders are empowered to dismiss complaints within 14 days and to determine whether a complaint is credible. Service members found to have filed false or repeatedly frivolous complaints may be prosecuted under Article 107 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, facing up to five years of confinement, punitive discharge, reduction in rank and forfeiture of pay, while civilian employees face expedited seven-day terminations. The policy was issued days after Hegseth announced a cut of 20% of general officers.

Off-duty ICE agent charged with felony assault after being shot by Fresno homeowner

tags: immigration, legal
sources: @aaronparnas

An ICE agent deployed to California as part of an enforcement surge was found asleep and apparently intoxicated on the lawn of a Fresno home, according to the New York Times. When the homeowner's father came outside, the agent got up and assaulted him, causing visible injuries, and then assaulted his daughter. The father shot the agent, and the daughter's boyfriend, a police officer, arrested him. The agent, who is from Texas, now faces felony assault and vandalism charges; the family did not know he was an ICE agent.

Musk PAC collecting voter data through texts and votesafe.org, officials say

tags: politics, privacy
sources: @aaronparnas

County officials in Colorado and Washington say a political action committee backed by Elon Musk has been spreading misinformation to voters and collecting personal information through a website called votesafe.org. CNN confirmed that Colorado voters received texts saying their ballot request was in and urging them to confirm where and when to return it, though every registered voter in the state already receives a mail-in ballot. Clicking the link routes voters' information to the PAC, and millions of dollars in digital advertising is driving traffic to the site, where users are asked to enter their address to check their registration.

Nine killed in Erie mass shooting as yearly total passes 365

tags: policing
sources: @aaronparnas

Nine people, including two children, were confirmed dead after a standoff and shooting inside a home on Perry Street in Erie, Pennsylvania, with police called to the scene around 5 p.m. Eastern. Eyewitnesses reported seeing a man firing a weapon. Two other mass shootings occurred in the same 24-hour period: two killed and two injured in Baltimore, Maryland, and four injured in Meridianville, Alabama. The United States has now recorded 365 mass shootings this year, more than the number of days elapsed.

Utah residents organize against data centers over bills, health and closed-door approvals

tags: tech, climate, politics
sources: @carolinegleich

Opposition to new data centers is drawing farmers, hunters, retirees and climate activists to the same county hearings, driven by rising utility bills that averaged $280 a month this year with one in six households behind on payments. Business Insider found that already-permitted data centers, if brought online, could cause up to 595 premature deaths and 300,000 asthma cases annually, as most new power comes from coal, oil and gas. In Box Elder County, commissioners refused public comment and approved the Stratos data center in a private room; local residents formed the Box Elder Accountability Referendum and filed a referendum petition the next morning, which the county denied and is now contesting in court. When the project's water application came up, 3,800 Utahns paid $15 each to protest it and the company withdrew it. Oregon has raised data center rates while lowering household rates, and Minnesota has barred utilities from passing data center costs to regular customers.

Guilfoyle asked GOP donor to wire $100,000 before confirmation hearing, report says

tags: politics, legal
sources: @groundnews

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle allegedly asked Republican donor Eric Deters to pay off $100,000 in credit card debt in exchange for access to the Trump administration, six days before her July 2025 Senate confirmation hearing, according to the Wall Street Journal. Text messages reviewed by CBS News show Guilfoyle saying a wire to her American Express account would not show up anywhere. Deters, who described the arrangement as quid pro quo, said he never sent the money and that he had previously paid Guilfoyle $300,000 for appearances, Donald Trump Jr. $200,000 and Eric Trump $100,000, and had sought her help reaching administration officials about a surgeon accused of health care fraud. Guilfoyle's attorney questioned the messages' authenticity, while sources told CBS News the White House had been told they were authentic; Marco Rubio and JD Vance both said they did not know the details.

Republican congressman to force House vote banning Russian oil purchases

tags: politics, markets
sources: @aaronparnas

Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania said he will introduce bipartisan legislation, the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act, to block all purchases of Russian oil following the administration's deal with Vladimir Putin. Fitzpatrick said the bill will be forced to the House floor via a discharge petition, which requires 218 signatures and bypasses the Speaker, and that he expects it to pass overwhelmingly. The president has described the oil arrangement as a major win, though critics note the volume involved is small relative to U.S. consumption.

Anonymous ICE investigator blames surge hiring and cut training for shootings

tags: immigration, policing
sources: @oafnation_actual

An anonymous veteran Homeland Security Investigations agent said HSI personnel are furious about recent shootings by ICE's Enforcement and Removal Operations branch, attributing the chaos to reduced vetting and training during the post-2025 hiring surge. The agent said an ERO officer who shot and killed a man with his child in the car in Maine in July was a surge hire with a history of domestic violence who would not have passed a standard background investigation. On the New York City shooting of Oscar Belgal, in which a child was in the car and DHS Secretary Mullin blamed the target, the agent said blame belongs with the officers and that there were many other opportunities to make the arrest. The agent also said HSI staff are being mistaken for immigration enforcement by the public and rejected Mayor Mamdani's call to abolish ICE.

Ex-CIA official pleads guilty to defrauding government of $194 million

tags: legal
sources: @groundnews

Former senior CIA official David J. Rush pleaded guilty to wire fraud in Virginia after inventing classified operations to obtain roughly $145 million for four luxury Florida properties and more than $40 million in gold. Prosecutors said he also falsified military and academic credentials, claimed tens of thousands of dollars in military leave compensation after his 2015 discharge, and attempted to release another $100 million from a government contract. Investigators seized about 300 gold bars, $2 million in cash and 35 luxury watches from his home. Rush is detained without bond and faces sentencing on January 28.

Utah to let AI prescribe acne medication without direct physician approval

tags: health, tech
sources: @groundnews

Utah has launched a one-year pilot allowing Nolla Health's AI system to assess patients with mild-to-moderate acne and issue prescriptions without direct physician approval, the first such state program. Patients pay $4.99 per month, scan their face and submit medical history through an app, after which the system assigns a severity score and selects from eight approved topical treatments. Doctors will review the first 100 prescriptions before they reach pharmacies and the next 400 on weekly retrospective review, after which physicians will review at least 10% of prescriptions monthly. Nolla Health CEO Luis Wenus said the approved medications are limited to topicals with side effects such as skin irritation or dryness.

US household water costs up 62% over a decade

tags: economy, climate
sources: @groundnews

Household water costs in the United States have risen 62% over the past decade, with the average annual bill reaching $531 in 2025, according to a study by Food and Water Watch based on 500 water systems serving 155 million people. Costs ranged from $133 a year in Hempstead, New York, to $1,416 in San Jose, California, with privately owned utilities charging an average of $823 compared with $494 for public systems. The increases come as utilities face aging infrastructure, climate adaptation costs and reduced federal funding. An EPA survey estimated that U.S. drinking water systems need $625 billion in infrastructure investment.

Administration begins felling more than 500 trees at East Potomac site in DC

tags: environment, politics
sources: @aaronparnas

The Trump administration has begun removing upwards of 500 trees at the East Potomac Golf Course in Washington, D.C., according to the Washington Post. Residents and observers on the ground say the trees are healthy oaks and maples, not dying or invasive specimens. The National Park Service says the removals are part of an effort to restore East Potomac. Residents across the city have objected to the scale of the clearing.

Man facing child rape charges set to become Louisiana police chief unopposed

tags: policing, legal
sources: @aaronparnas

Christopher Paul, a Republican running unopposed for city police chief in Elizabeth, Louisiana, is currently facing two counts of second-degree rape, according to the Guardian. The charges relate to allegations involving two 13-year-old girls roughly 20 years ago, with a complaint filed in August of this year. The only other candidate in the race dropped out. Some residents have argued the position should be converted from an elected one to an appointed one.

Palm Beach mayoral candidate posts Israeli DNA test denying he is Jeffrey Epstein

tags: politics, legal
sources: @hunteralexanderhowell

A Palm Beach mayoral candidate known as Palm Beach Pete posted a genetic identity verification report from Biogenesis Solutions in Tel Aviv, Israel, concluding that he is not Jeffrey Epstein. In an accompanying statement he said he had just returned from Israel, praised the country's technology as decades ahead, and said the establishment is targeting him because he is running for mayor.

Monitored wildlife populations fell 73% between 1970 and 2022

tags: climate, environment
sources: @groundnews

Wildlife populations monitored worldwide declined by an average of 73% between 1970 and 2022, according to the World Wide Fund for Nature's 2026 Living Planet Report, which tracked 35,803 populations across 5,790 species of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish. Freshwater populations saw the largest average decline at 85%, followed by land species at 69% and marine species at 59%. South America recorded a 95% decline compared with 80% in Africa. Habitat destruction was the most reported threat, alongside climate change, pollution and overexploitation, and researchers cautioned the figure reflects average population declines rather than the share of individual animals lost.

World's largest penguin colony shrinks 63% in 14 years

tags: climate, environment
sources: @groundnews

Zavodovski Island near Antarctica has lost its status as the world's largest penguin colony after its chinstrap penguin population fell 63%, from 1.09 million breeding individuals in 2011 to 402,000 in 2025, according to a British Antarctic Survey study. Researchers linked the decline to climate change pushing krill, the penguins' main food source, toward colder southern waters, and ruled out a 2016 volcanic eruption as the main cause. The island's macaroni penguin population rose from 338,000 to 433,000 over the same period. Scientists recommended reclassifying chinstrap penguins from least concern to endangered; Cape Adare, with over one million Adélie penguins, now holds the title of largest colony.

UN report finds 68% of Myanmar's population poor or at risk

tags: economy, politics
sources: @groundnews

More than 37 million people in Myanmar, or 68% of the population, live in poverty or face the risk of falling into it, according to a United Nations Development Program report based on a survey of 7,463 households. Nearly 18 million people are classified as poor and another 19.5 million as vulnerable. Limited access to healthcare, housing, clean water and sanitation accounts for most measured poverty, with conditions worst in conflict-affected regions. Myanmar has faced armed conflict and economic instability since the military overthrew Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in 2021, and the UNDP estimates at least one million young people may have left the country since.

Speaker tells European Parliament audience coronavirus research was weapons development

tags: health, politics
sources: @ericmoutsos

In remarks delivered at the European Union Parliament, a speaker argued that the COVID-19 pandemic was the product of decades of deliberate biological engineering rather than a natural event. He cited the 1965 isolation of coronavirus, 1966-67 transatlantic experiments, Pfizer's 1990 spike protein vaccine patent, a 2002 University of North Carolina patent on an infectious replication-defective coronavirus clone funded by Anthony Fauci's NIAID, and a 2003 CDC patent on SARS coronavirus isolated from humans, which he said violated biological and chemical weapons treaties. He also pointed to a 2014 exemption from the gain-of-function moratorium, a 2016 paper describing WIV1 as poised for human emergence, and April 2019 amendments to four Moderna patent applications referencing the accidental or intentional release of a respiratory pathogen. He said the published literature from 1990 to 2018 consistently found that coronavirus mutates too quickly for vaccines to be effective.
